Visually demonstrate how ISE authenticates a user, assigns an SGT, and how that SGT is embedded in the VXLAN header. screens.title: Policy Enforcement with Cisco TrustSec and ISE
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how Cisco TrustSec and Identity Services Engine work together to move policy from brittle IP lists to identity-driven controls. TrustSec introduces Security Group Tags: compact 16-bit identifiers that label users and devices by role. ISE authenticates endpoints, decides what they should be allowed to do, and assigns an SGT to each session. That SGT travels inside the SD-Access overlay so fabric devices can enforce policies without depending on addresses or physical topology. We'll follow a user from authentication through SGT assignment, show how SGACLs encode permit and deny rules between groups, and explain how DNA Center and ISE distribute that policy to Fabric Edge and Border nodes. You will also see common pitfalls — like RADIUS misconfiguration or overly broad SGACLs — and practical testing steps to verify SGT propagation. By the end you will be able to explain why identity-based segmentation simplifies policy management and how SGTs enable precise micro-segmentation that follows the user across the fabric.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over these screens you will build a practical understanding of identity-based segmentation and how ISE and TrustSec realize it. First, you will learn to explain the core principles of TrustSec and why SGTs replace many IP-based ACLs. Second, you'll learn how ISE performs authentication and authorization, and how SGT assignment is communicated to fabric nodes. Third, you'll practice configuring identity-based policies in the form of SGACLs and understand the format of a policy matrix. Finally, you'll trace SGT flow from an authentication event through the data path so you can validate enforcement with show commands and DNA Center Assurance. Each objective ties to hands-on verification steps: reading assigned SGTs in ISE, confirming SGT propagation in fabric device caches, and testing permit and deny behaviors. These skills matter because they let you design policies that scale with people and devices instead of with addresses, reducing configuration churn and improving micro-segmentation. By the end you'll be ready to map user roles to SGTs and verify that policies are correctly enforced across the fabric.

screens.title: Why identity-based policy beats IP ACLs
screens.narratorSegment: Traditional IP-based ACLs tie policy to addresses and topology. That creates heavy operational churn: when users move, addresses change, and ACLs need updates. Identity-based policy, implemented by TrustSec and ISE, decouples policy from IP. Instead you define rules between logical groups identified by Security Group Tags. For example, instead of permitting a range of IP addresses to reach a server, you permit the Employees SGT to reach the Servers SGT. This matters because policies then follow the person or device as they roam, greatly reducing the number of ACL entries you manage. A common misconception is that SGTs replace all network controls; they do not remove underlay requirements. You still need correct underlay routing, VXLAN, and LISP for endpoint reachability. Another pitfall is assuming SGTs automatically enforce encryption or external routing — they control access policy, not routing protocols. Concretely, in a campus where contractors frequently change desks, SGT-based policy avoids repeated address-based edits. Your takeaway: identity-based policy reduces configuration churn and enables micro-segmentation, but you must pair it with a healthy underlay and sound SGACL design. Why identity-based policy beats IP ACLs means sgts let policies follow identity rather than ip, lowering operational cost and enabling granular micro-segmentation.. In practical terms, the shift from address-based rules to role-based controls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison › Identity vs IP-based
Identity-based policy vs IP ACLs
Why SGTs simplify segmentation and where they still need supporting systems
IP-based ACLs (traditional)
  • Policies tied to IP addresses and subnets.
  • High maintenance when endpoints move or addresses change.
  • Scaling problems with many ACL entries for dynamic environments.
  • Example: update ACL when a user is assigned a new IP.
Common mistake
Assuming IP ACLs are simpler when users roam; they are not — they add operational overhead.
Identity-based (TrustSec + ISE)
  • Policies defined between logical groups identified by SGTs.
  • Policies follow users or devices as they attach anywhere in the fabric.
  • Enables micro-segmentation and reduces ACL churn.
  • Example: permit Employees SGT to Servers SGT regardless of IP.
Key takeaway
Use SGTs to express intent; keep underlay and device capability in mind.

screens.title: Security Group Tags (SGTs)
screens.narratorSegment: A Security Group Tag is a compact identifier that represents a logical group of users or devices with the same access requirements. The chapter emphasizes that an SGT is a 16-bit value — that numeric tag is the label your policies refer to. You assign SGTs to meaningful roles like Employees, Guests, or Servers. ISE assigns the correct SGT during authorization, and then the fabric carries that value in the VXLAN overlay so enforcement can occur anywhere in the fabric. A common misconception is to treat SGTs like encryption keys or routing identifiers. They are neither: SGTs are policy labels. Another practical consideration is consistent mapping: pick an SGT numbering plan that aligns with organizational roles and document it. For example, SGT 10 for Employees, 20 for Guests, 30 for Servers is the sample mapping used in the chapter. Your takeaway: SGTs are the fundamental identity token for TrustSec policies — once endpoints are tagged, enforcement becomes a simple lookup against SGACLs. Security Group Tags (SGTs) means an sgt is a 16-bit identity tag assigned by ise to group endpoints for policy; it is a label used by sgacls for enforcement.. In practical terms, what an sgt is, how it represents identity, and why it's 16 bits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept › Security Group Tag
What is a Security Group Tag?
A compact label assigned to a user or device that represents its logical security group.
Definition and role

An SGT is a 16-bit number assigned by ISE during authorization. It classifies an endpoint into a logical group used by SGACLs to determine permitted or denied traffic. The tag is carried inside the VXLAN overlay so enforcement is independent of IP address or attachment point.

Example mapping
  • SGT 10 — Employees
  • SGT 20 — Guests
  • SGT 30 — Servers
Misconception
SGTs are not routing identifiers; they are policy labels used for access control decisions.
How SGTs travel
Once assigned, the SGT is inserted into the VXLAN header of overlay traffic. Fabric Edge Nodes read that tag and apply SGACLs accordingly at the destination edge.
Why 16 bits? It provides a compact namespace large enough for hundreds of groups while keeping the overlay header small.

screens.title: ISE: Authentication, Authorization, and SGT Assignment
screens.narratorSegment: ISE serves as the central policy decision point in an SD-Access deployment. Its AAA role includes verifying identity, deciding access rights, and assigning an SGT to the session. Authentication can be performed with 802.1X, MAC Authentication Bypass, or web authentication methods. During authorization ISE evaluates policies and chooses the correct SGT; this decision is communicated to the Fabric Edge Node via RADIUS. ISE also stores SGACLs as the policy repository, so it becomes the single source of truth for who may talk to whom. A typical process is: a device authenticates, ISE authorizes and selects an SGT, ISE replies over RADIUS with the assigned tag, the Fabric Edge Node tags the endpoint traffic, and the tag is used by destination nodes to apply SGACLs. A common mistake is misconfiguring the RADIUS shared secret between ISE and fabric devices which prevents SGT delivery. Your practical check: after authentication, confirm the assigned SGT in ISE and verify the fabric node learned the tag. That ensures policy enforcement will work end-to-end. ISE: Authentication, Authorization, and SGT Assignment means ise authenticates and authorizes endpoints, assigns sgts via radius, and stores sgacls that define inter-group access rules.. In practical terms, how ise decides and delegates identity information. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ISE responsibilities
keyIdea.text: ISE authenticates and authorizes endpoints, assigns SGTs via RADIUS, and stores SGACLs that define inter-group access rules.

content.html:
Process Flow › ISE AAA & SGT
ISE: Authentication → Authorization → SGT
Step-by-step lifecycle of identity and tag assignment
  1. Authentication: Device or user authenticates using 802.1X, MAB, or web auth.
  2. Authorization: ISE evaluates policies and maps the session to an SGT.
  3. SGT assignment: ISE returns the SGT to the Fabric Edge Node via RADIUS attributes.
  4. Tagging: The Fabric Edge Node tags traffic with the SGT in the VXLAN header.
  5. Enforcement: Destination fabric nodes consult SGACLs to permit or deny flows based on SGTs.
Pro tip
Confirm the RADIUS attributes in ISE are mapped correctly to the SGT attribute expected by the fabric to avoid tag delivery failures.
Concrete example
A laptop authenticates via 802.1X. ISE authorizes the user as an Employee and assigns SGT 10. The switch receives the assigned tag and marks overlay traffic. When the laptop connects to a server, the server's edge node uses the SGACL between SGT 10 and SGT 30 to decide access.
Misconception: if authentication succeeds but RADIUS attributes fail, the endpoint may be authenticated but untagged — policy enforcement will not function as intended.

screens.title: How SGTs are propagated in the SD-Access fabric
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter explains the path SGT information takes after ISE assigns a tag. Once ISE decides the SGT, it sends that information to the Fabric Edge Node using RADIUS. The Fabric Edge Node then tags all overlay traffic from that endpoint by inserting the SGT into the VXLAN header. This allows any destination Fabric Edge Node or Border Node that receives the traffic to read the tag and apply the appropriate SGACL. DNA Center plays a supporting role by pushing TrustSec configuration so devices understand the SGT values and local policy caches are populated. A common misconception is to expect SGTs to be part of the underlay — they are carried only in the overlay. If a device in the fabric cannot process SGTs, it cannot enforce SGACLs even if ISE assigned the tag. Practical verification includes checking the device's SGT cache and using Assurance tools like path trace to confirm the tag is present in transit. The key operational concern is that both ISE and fabric devices must be configured consistently and able to exchange RADIUS and TrustSec information.

keyIdea.title: Propagation summary
keyIdea.text: ISE assigns the SGT, sends it via RADIUS to the edge, the edge inserts the tag into VXLAN, and destination nodes use SGACLs to enforce policy.

content.html:
Architecture › SGT propagation
SGT propagation through the fabric
How tag information travels and where enforcement happens
Flow summary

1. ISE assigns SGT during authorization and returns it via RADIUS.

2. Fabric Edge Node receives the SGT and tags the endpoint's overlay traffic in the VXLAN header.

3. When traffic arrives at the destination fabric node, the node consults its local SGACL cache to permit or deny traffic based on the source and destination SGTs.

4. DNA Center helps by pushing TrustSec configuration so devices understand SGT mappings and SGACLs.

Operational note
If any device in this chain cannot process SGTs, enforcement will fail; ensure hardware capability and consistent configuration across the fabric.
Checkpoints
  • ISE shows assigned SGT for the session.
  • Edge node SGT cache contains the mapping.
  • Path Trace confirms the SGT in transit and SGACL application.

screens.title: Security Group Access Control Lists (SGACLs)
screens.narratorSegment: SGACLs are the policy constructs that define permitted or denied traffic between two Security Group Tags. The chapter presents SGACLs as a matrix: rows are source SGTs and columns are destination SGTs, with entries showing permit or deny rules and specific service exceptions like HTTP or RDP. For example, Employees to Servers may permit TCP 80 and 443, whereas Guests to Servers may be denied. SGACLs live in ISE as the authoritative policy repository and are pushed to fabric devices so enforcement can be performed locally at the edge. A misconception to avoid is assuming SGACLs automatically log or inspect application payloads; they control connectivity by SGT pairs and ports. When designing SGACLs, follow least privilege: deny by default and explicitly permit required services. Also avoid overly broad permits which can reintroduce lateral movement risk. Your practical step is to model the matrix for your organization, map services to permit entries, test in lab, and then push via DNA Center while monitoring enforcement in Assurance tools. Security Group Access Control Lists (SGACLs) means sgacls define the allow/deny rules between sgt pairs and are the operational expression of identity-based policy stored in ise.. In practical terms, policy matrices that control flow between sgts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › SGACL Matrix
Security Group Access Control Lists
A matrix of policy entries that govern traffic between SGTs
Sample matrix (excerpt)
Source \/ Dest Employees (SGT 10) Guests (SGT 20) Servers (SGT 30)
Employees — Deny IP Permit TCP 80, 443, 3389
Guests Deny IP — Deny IP
Servers Deny IP Deny IP Deny IP (no initiate)
Design guidance
  • Start with deny-by-default and add explicit permits for needed services.
  • Keep service exceptions specific to ports and protocols where possible.
  • Test changes in a lab before pushing to production.
Key takeaway
Treat the SGACL matrix as the canonical policy document and keep it versioned and tested.

screens.title: Troubleshooting SGT and SGACL issues
screens.narratorSegment: When policies do not behave as expected, the chapter recommends a sequence of focused checks. First, confirm the endpoint authentication status in ISE and verify the assigned SGT. If ISE shows the correct SGT but the fabric does not enforce policy, check the RADIUS shared secret and attribute mapping between ISE and the fabric device. Next, inspect the fabric device's SGT cache to confirm it learned the mapping. Useful show commands include: show cts sgt-map to see SGT to endpoint mappings and show cts role-based permissions to view locally cached SGACL entries. Another good test is a path trace from DNA Center to confirm the SGT is propagated and the SGACL applied. A common pitfall is overly broad SGACLs; when you see unexpected access, check matrix entries for permissive rules. Finally, ensure ISE is highly available and backed up because it is the single policy decision point. These practical checks help you isolate whether the problem is authentication, tag delivery, policy configuration, or device capability. Troubleshooting SGT and SGACL issues means verify authentication in ise, confirm sgt assignment, check radius and device caches, then use path trace to validate sgacl application.. In practical terms, checks, show commands, and common configuration pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Designing a simple SGACL policy matrix
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter includes an activity to design an SGACL matrix for a small fabric. You are given SGTs for Developers, HR Staff, Development Servers, HR Servers, and Internet. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how Cisco TrustSec and Identity Services Engine work together to move policy from brittle IP lists to identity-driven controls. TrustSec introduces Security Group Tags: compact 16-bit identifiers that label users and devices by role. ISE authenticates endpoints, decides what they should be allowed to do, and assigns an SGT to each session. That SGT travels inside the SD-Access overlay so fabric devices can enforce policies without depending on addresses or physical topology. We'll follow a user from authentication through SGT assignment, show how SGACLs encode permit and deny rules between groups, and explain how DNA Center and ISE distribute that policy to Fabric Edge and Border nodes. You will also see common pitfalls — like RADIUS misconfiguration or overly broad SGACLs — and practical testing steps to verify SGT propagation. By the end you will be able to explain why identity-based segmentation simplifies policy management and how SGTs enable precise micro-segmentation that follows the user across the fabric.

Over these screens you will build a practical understanding of identity-based segmentation and how ISE and TrustSec realize it. First, you will learn to explain the core principles of TrustSec and why SGTs replace many IP-based ACLs. Second, you'll learn how ISE performs authentication and authorization, and how SGT assignment is communicated to fabric nodes. Third, you'll practice configuring identity-based policies in the form of SGACLs and understand the format of a policy matrix. Finally, you'll trace SGT flow from an authentication event through the data path so you can validate enforcement with show commands and DNA Center Assurance. Each objective ties to hands-on verification steps: reading assigned SGTs in ISE, confirming SGT propagation in fabric device caches, and testing permit and deny behaviors. These skills matter because they let you design policies that scale with people and devices instead of with addresses, reducing configuration churn and improving micro-segmentation. By the end you'll be ready to map user roles to SGTs and verify that policies are correctly enforced across the fabric.

These second set of objectives focuses on concrete configuration and troubleshooting actions you'll perform. You will learn how to map real user roles to SGT values and how DNA Center distributes TrustSec configuration to fabric devices. Next, you'll practice interpreting an SGACL matrix and translating it into rules applied by fabric nodes. You will also learn to identify common mistakes such as incorrect RADIUS shared secrets or overly permissive SGACL entries, and the practical steps to correct them. Finally, you'll run verification steps: check endpoint authentication state in ISE, read the assigned SGT, use fabric device show commands to confirm SGT maps, and run a path trace to verify SGACL application. Each objective links a configuration step to a verification technique so that you can confidently test policy behavior in a lab before deploying to production. These skills reduce risk and make policy changes safe and reversible.

Traditional IP-based ACLs tie policy to addresses and topology. That creates heavy operational churn: when users move, addresses change, and ACLs need updates. Identity-based policy, implemented by TrustSec and ISE, decouples policy from IP. Instead you define rules between logical groups identified by Security Group Tags. For example, instead of permitting a range of IP addresses to reach a server, you permit the Employees SGT to reach the Servers SGT. This matters because policies then follow the person or device as they roam, greatly reducing the number of ACL entries you manage. A common misconception is that SGTs replace all network controls; they do not remove underlay requirements. You still need correct underlay routing, VXLAN, and LISP for endpoint reachability. Another pitfall is assuming SGTs automatically enforce encryption or external routing — they control access policy, not routing protocols. Concretely, in a campus where contractors frequently change desks, SGT-based policy avoids repeated address-based edits. Your takeaway: identity-based policy reduces configuration churn and enables micro-segmentation, but you must pair it with a healthy underlay and sound SGACL design. Why identity-based policy beats IP ACLs means sgts let policies follow identity rather than ip, lowering operational cost and enabling granular micro-segmentation.. In practical terms, the shift from address-based rules to role-based controls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Security Group Tag is a compact identifier that represents a logical group of users or devices with the same access requirements. The chapter emphasizes that an SGT is a 16-bit value — that numeric tag is the label your policies refer to. You assign SGTs to meaningful roles like Employees, Guests, or Servers. ISE assigns the correct SGT during authorization, and then the fabric carries that value in the VXLAN overlay so enforcement can occur anywhere in the fabric. A common misconception is to treat SGTs like encryption keys or routing identifiers. They are neither: SGTs are policy labels. Another practical consideration is consistent mapping: pick an SGT numbering plan that aligns with organizational roles and document it. For example, SGT 10 for Employees, 20 for Guests, 30 for Servers is the sample mapping used in the chapter. Your takeaway: SGTs are the fundamental identity token for TrustSec policies — once endpoints are tagged, enforcement becomes a simple lookup against SGACLs. Security Group Tags (SGTs) means an sgt is a 16-bit identity tag assigned by ise to group endpoints for policy; it is a label used by sgacls for enforcement.. In practical terms, what an sgt is, how it represents identity, and why it's 16 bits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

ISE serves as the central policy decision point in an SD-Access deployment. Its AAA role includes verifying identity, deciding access rights, and assigning an SGT to the session. Authentication can be performed with 802.1X, MAC Authentication Bypass, or web authentication methods. During authorization ISE evaluates policies and chooses the correct SGT; this decision is communicated to the Fabric Edge Node via RADIUS. ISE also stores SGACLs as the policy repository, so it becomes the single source of truth for who may talk to whom. A typical process is: a device authenticates, ISE authorizes and selects an SGT, ISE replies over RADIUS with the assigned tag, the Fabric Edge Node tags the endpoint traffic, and the tag is used by destination nodes to apply SGACLs. A common mistake is misconfiguring the RADIUS shared secret between ISE and fabric devices which prevents SGT delivery. Your practical check: after authentication, confirm the assigned SGT in ISE and verify the fabric node learned the tag. That ensures policy enforcement will work end-to-end. ISE: Authentication, Authorization, and SGT Assignment means ise authenticates and authorizes endpoints, assigns sgts via radius, and stores sgacls that define inter-group access rules.. In practical terms, how ise decides and delegates identity information. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The chapter explains the path SGT information takes after ISE assigns a tag. Once ISE decides the SGT, it sends that information to the Fabric Edge Node using RADIUS. The Fabric Edge Node then tags all overlay traffic from that endpoint by inserting the SGT into the VXLAN header. This allows any destination Fabric Edge Node or Border Node that receives the traffic to read the tag and apply the appropriate SGACL. DNA Center plays a supporting role by pushing TrustSec configuration so devices understand the SGT values and local policy caches are populated. A common misconception is to expect SGTs to be part of the underlay — they are carried only in the overlay. If a device in the fabric cannot process SGTs, it cannot enforce SGACLs even if ISE assigned the tag. Practical verification includes checking the device's SGT cache and using Assurance tools like path trace to confirm the tag is present in transit. The key operational concern is that both ISE and fabric devices must be configured consistently and able to exchange RADIUS and TrustSec information.

SGACLs are the policy constructs that define permitted or denied traffic between two Security Group Tags. The chapter presents SGACLs as a matrix: rows are source SGTs and columns are destination SGTs, with entries showing permit or deny rules and specific service exceptions like HTTP or RDP. For example, Employees to Servers may permit TCP 80 and 443, whereas Guests to Servers may be denied. SGACLs live in ISE as the authoritative policy repository and are pushed to fabric devices so enforcement can be performed locally at the edge. A misconception to avoid is assuming SGACLs automatically log or inspect application payloads; they control connectivity by SGT pairs and ports. When designing SGACLs, follow least privilege: deny by default and explicitly permit required services. Also avoid overly broad permits which can reintroduce lateral movement risk. Your practical step is to model the matrix for your organization, map services to permit entries, test in lab, and then push via DNA Center while monitoring enforcement in Assurance tools. Security Group Access Control Lists (SGACLs) means sgacls define the allow/deny rules between sgt pairs and are the operational expression of identity-based policy stored in ise.. In practical terms, policy matrices that control flow between sgts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's summarize three essential concepts you must remember. First, Cisco TrustSec and SGTs enable identity-based segmentation by labeling endpoints with compact 16-bit tags. Second, ISE is the policy decision point: it authenticates endpoints, authorizes access, assigns SGTs via RADIUS, and stores SGACLs which define who may talk to whom. Third, SGACLs are the operational matrix that fabric devices use to permit or deny traffic between SGT pairs. Together these elements let you define policy by role instead of by address and enable true micro-segmentation.
